steps.title: Notgroschen
steps.body: The "emergency penny": money kept aside for when something breaks or a job ends. It's an [[emergency-fund]]. Its job isn't to grow. Its job is to be there at once, so nothing has to be sold or borrowed in a hurry.

steps.prompt: The family's costs are €2,800 a month. How big is a buffer for 3 months?
steps.reveal: 3 × €2,800 = €8,400. A buffer is counted in months of costs, not in a round number. With one income gone, it buys time to find the next job.

items.text: Three months of costs if a job ends

steps.explanation: Money needed soon has a short [[time-horizon]]: it has to be there, whatever markets do. Money that can wait decades has time to ride out falls.

steps.prompt: Why does a buffer belong somewhere it can't fall, even if it earns little?
options: It's needed exactly when things go wrong, maybe while markets are down too
Because savings accounts pay the most
Because a buffer should grow as fast as possible
steps.explanation: Job losses and market falls often come together. A buffer that has dropped 20% when you need it has failed at its one job.

t1.body: It means "emergency penny": money for when something breaks or a job ends. In English: an [[emergency-fund]]. It doesn't need to grow. It needs to be there right away, so you don't have to sell or borrow in a hurry.
